In this lesson you will learn about a very important circuit, the 555 timer.
INTRODUCTIONM
The 555 timer is a circuit that provides timing signals to other digital circuits.
The importance of accurate timing in digital systems cannot be overemphasized.
Without accurate timing, everyday appliances such as TVs, VCRs, stereos and even cars would not be able to function.
>DFFGMNNOR
A low cost, effective digital timer had to be developed as digital circuitry became commonplace.
The 555 Timer (and its revisions) is that digital circuit..

LESSON MENU
The 555 integrated circuit is a commonly used device that operates as either an astable or monostable vibrator.
DISCUSSION
The output waveform is a square wave that can range from a few hertz to several megahertz.
555 timers can operate as TTL compatible astable multivibrators, monostable multivibrators, pulse width modulators, pulse position modulators or linear ramp generators.
Most 555 integrated circuits are housed in an eight-pin dip case.
Some older style 555's are housed in cans.

The internal circuit design is what makes the 555 versatile. Let's discuss the internal operation.
The major components of the 555 timer are an inverter, a transistor, 2 comparators and an RS flip-flop..
Together, the circuit can operate in many configurations.
Let's briefly discuss the comparators and RS flip-flop operation.
A comparator does what its name implies, it compares two input voltage levels.
If the + input is larger than the - input, the output is high (1 or true).
If the + input is smaller than the - input, the output is low (0 or false).
Notice the - input is subtracted from the + input. If the difference is 1 or positive the output is 1. If the difference is 0 or negative the output is 0.
RS flip-flop operation is just as simple. RS means Reset, Set.
The device has three inputs:...............................
The outputs are always opposite. If Q is 1, Q is 0 and if Q is 0, Q is 1.
If the S input (SET) is high, Q is high and Q is low. The flip-flop is said to be SET.
If the R input (RESET) is high, Q is low and Q is high. The flip-flop is RESET.
Having R and S high at the same time will drive both Q and Q low, this is an invalid input condition.
Once the flip-flop is SET or RESET, the outputs will not change if the inputs become zero.
The flip-flop stays SET or RESET until a high is present on an input.
The CLR input overrides inputs R and S. If CLR is low, the flip-flop resets, (Q low and Q high) even if input S is high.
The small circle on the CLR input indicates a low activates this function.
As long as CLR is high, the flip-flop SETs when S is high and RESETs when R is high...
What is the output of this comparator?
Notice the - input is larger than the + input. To determine whether the input is high or low subtract the negative input from the positive.

Note that the 555 by itself will not operate, it takes external components connected to pins 2, 4, 5, 6, and 7.
You can see how different voltages on pins 2, 4, 5, 6 and 7 affect the circuits without seeing the connected components.
The R and S inputs to the flip-flop are provided by the outputs of two comparators.
When the output of a comparator becomes high, the flip-flop will SET or RESET depending on which comparator has the high output.
Remember, a zero or low input to the RS flip-flop has no effect, the flip-flop stays SET or RESET.
The CLR input to the flip-flop comes from an external source.
In most configurations, the CLR input is tied to Vcc which disables CLR.
The comparators have a reference voltage applied from +Vcc.
+Vcc is divided by three equal value resistors and applied to comparators 1 and 2...........
2/3 of +Vcc is applied to the - input of comparator 1.
Also note that this voltage can be changed by applying a voltage to the control input on Pin 5. This adds versatility to the chip.
In most configurations, Pin 5 is connected to ground through a DC blocking capacitor (blocks 2/3 +Vcc from ground).
1/3 of Vcc is applied to the + input of comparator 2.
These reference voltages and the inputs on pins 6 (threshold) and 2 (trigger) make the 555 operate.
The external components connected to pins 2 and 6 control the 555 timer configuration.
When the threshold voltage input, on Pin 6, goes above 2/3 Vcc, comparator 1 produces a high output that is applied to the R input of the flip-flop.
The RS flip-flop resets causing the Q output to go high. The inverter changes the high to a low and puts a low on pin 3.
Even if the threshold voltage drops below 2/3 Vcc and causes a low output from comparator 1, the flip-flop stays RESET.
When the trigger input voltage, on Pin 2 drops below 1/3 Vcc, comparator 2 puts a high on input S of the flip-flop.
The high from comparator 2 causes the flip-flop to SET, Q goes low and the output becomes high.
Even if the trigger input goes above 1/3 Vcc, the 0 output of comparator 2 will not change the flip-flop's state.
To summarize, Pin 3 output is LOW when the threshold input goes above 2/3 Vcc and HIGH when the trigger input goes below 1/3 of Vcc.... of Vcc.
Note that when the 555 output goes low, it stays low even if the voltage on the threshold input drops below 2/3 Vcc.
When the 555 output is high, it stays high even if the voltage on the trigger input goes above 1/3 Vcc.
The transistor in the 555 timer performs another important operation.
The transistor is used as a switch to supply a ground to Pin 7, the Discharge pin.
When the Q output of the flip-flop is high, the transistor is forward biased, connecting the ground on Pin 1 to Pin 7.
When the Q output of the flip-flop is low, the transistor is reverse biased, breaking the connection from Pin 1 to Pin 7.
The operation of the threshold and trigger inputs along with the ground or no ground on the discharge pin are important for circuit operation.

The 555 timer can be configured for many types of circuits. The chip was designed to be very versatile.
DISCUSSION
We are going to discuss its use as an astable and monostable multivibrator.
The astable multivibrator is a circuit that produces a continuous square wave output. There are no stable states.
As long as power is applied to the circuit, there is an output square wave.
The monostable multivibrator is a circuit that produces a high output only when an input is received, then the output goes back low. There is one stable state.

The connection of R2 and C1 is applied to Pins 2 and 6, the threshold and trigger inputs.
The circuit operation is based on the charging and discharging of C1.

The cycle repeats. As long as power is applied to the circuit, the output is a continuous square wave.
The output is high until C1 charges above 2/3 Vcc. Then the output is low and a ground is placed on Pin 7 to discharge C1.
As C1 discharges, the output is low until the discharge is below 1/3 Vcc. Then the output goes high and the ground is removed from Pin 7 to charge C1.
The frequency of the output waveform depends on the charge and discharge time of C1 and the RC time constant.
Different values of R1, R2 and C1 will produce different output frequencies.

MONOSTABLE MULTIVIBRATOR CIRCUIT - External connection to 555 Timer.

Pin 1 and Pin 5 are grounded. Pin 5 at ground keeps the reference voltages at 2/3 and 1/3 Vcc.
The connection of R1 and C1 is applied to Pins 6 and 7. Pin 7 is open or grounded depending on the 555 circuit.
The circuit input is the Trigger, Pin 2, and is normally high. A low starts circuit operation.

MONOSTABLE MULTIVIBRATOR CIRCUIT - A high on comparator #2 causes a low output to the S input of the flip-flop. No change since the threshold hasn't reached 2/3 Vcc.
At just above 2/3 Vcc, the threshold input causes the output to go low and Pin 7 is grounded.
If the 555 circuit has a high output when power is first applied (either Q or Q will be high, which one is not predictable), the output returns to low..
With the ground on Pins 6 and 7, C1 quickly discharges to 0 volts. However, the output does not change.
MONOSTABLE MULTIVIBRATOR CIRCUIT - A low from Pin 6 causes a low to the R input of the flip-flop. No change since the trigger input hasn't changed to low.
As before, the circuit stays in the stable state until another input is received on the trigger.
The output stays low until a low input signal is received on the trigger.
The low trigger input causes a high output and the ground to be removed from Pins 6 and 7 allowing C1 to charge.
Once C1 charges above 2/3 Vcc, the output goes back to low and the ground is placed back on Pins 6 and 7.
The time the output is high depends on the time constant of R1 and C1, not the time Pin 2 is low. This is normal monostable operation.
Different values of R1 and C1 will produce different pulse lengths.

This experiment demonstrates the operation of a 555 timer in the astable and monostable modes. You will measure the output signal to verify correct circuit operation for various external component selections.
EXPERIMENT
The purpose of the PC130-153 card is to demonstrate the various operation modes of the 555 Timer.

Locate IC1, on the right hand side of the card. This is the 555 timer IC.
The test points numbered 1 through 8 correspond to the pins on the IC.
S1 is used to supply signals from an external source. When UP, the signal is applied to PIN 2, the trigger input on the 555. When DOWN, the signal is applied to Pin 5, the control input on the 555.

S3 selects RC time constants of either R2 and R3 (10k to 20k) or R4 (100k).
S4 selects between C2 (.01 mf) and C3 (1 mf) for changing the RC time constant of the circuit.
S5, when UP, supplies an external signal to the CLR input, Pin 4 of the 555.
S6 supplies a triggering voltage from the card to the trigger input in the monostable mode of operation.
